title: Professor Gurmukh Singh
hookLine: a teacher who pushed for Punjabi and Sikh education

lines: HOW WILL THEY READ THE GURU'S WORD?
cards: A classroom in Lahore. Chalk on the board. The language of government is English, the language of the courts is Urdu, and the language of the students' own homes, Punjabi, barely has a place in school.
Their teacher thinks that's a problem worth spending his life on. If Sikh children can't read Punjabi in the Gurmukhi letters, how will they read the Guru's word?
He's a professor and a reformer, and his reforms will cost him.

teach.b: First, the classroom. Gurmukh Singh taught at Oriental College in Lahore, and pressed for Punjabi to be taught properly, in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib.
A language that isn't taught in school slowly becomes a language only for the kitchen. Second, the organizer.
He was among the leaders of the Lahore Singh Sabha, and worked to link the Singh Sabhas into a wider council.
He started papers, gathered writers like Giani Ditt Singh, and argued for a Sikh college where young Sikhs could study modern subjects without losing their own tradition. Third, the price.
His plain teaching on equality angered powerful men in Amritsar, including some of honored lineage. Priests there issued an edict casting him out of the Panth. He kept teaching anyway.
Much later, the Akal Takht itself declared that edict void, restoring his name. The record was corrected, long after the man was gone. Fourth, what a teacher is in the Sikh tradition.
The word Sikh, Sikh teachers explain, means a learner, a disciple, and the Gurus are teachers. The Guru's hymns speak of the true Guru as the one who joins the seeker to the Name.
A human teacher isn't the Guru, but a good one points the way. Gurmukh Singh spent his life pointing young people toward their own language and their own scripture.

how: Sikhs remember Professor Gurmukh Singh as a Lahore teacher and Singh Sabha leader who pushed for Punjabi in Gurmukhi and for Sikh education, and whose excommunication the Akal Takht later declared void.

games.q: you're Gurmukh Singh. an edict from Amritsar casts you out of the Panth. what do you do?
o: keep teaching and working for Sikh education.
games.why: he kept teaching, and much later the Akal Takht declared the edict void.

practice: Think of one thing you know how to do well, a recipe, a song, a way of calming down, a few words of another language, and one person who might want to know it.
Picture yourself showing them slowly, the way a good teacher would, without hurry and without making them feel small. If you pray, let Waheguru fill the pauses between breaths.
